One fixed rule, a year of gold and Nasdaq futures. About three in four blocks were touched again. Of those, close to half held: gold about 48%, Nasdaq about 51%.

Not a wall. Closer to a coin that lands on its edge and then picks a side.

Past data, not a signal. Research, not advice.

It held. Your stop didn't.

About one in five order blocks that held, on both gold and Nasdaq, still stopped the trade out first. A wick dipped below the zone, took the stop, then price ran to the target.

Bigger size didn't help them pass.

An example trader, 20,000 simulated runs on a year of real sessions. Within 60 trading days, about 32% passed at one micro, 35% at two, 34% at three, and 30 to 33% at five, eight and ten.

Trading bigger did not make passing more likely. It just changed how quickly you found out.

Example numbers, not a prediction. Research, not advice.

fp-short-C.ig:
The maths behind a blown funded account.

At five micros with a $150 stop per micro, one stopped day costs $750. Three of those close together and a $2,000 line is gone.

At one micro, the same three days cost $450, and the next good week can repair it.

The target is fixed. The line is fixed. Size decides how many bad days you survive.

Example numbers. Research, not advice.

Full video on YouTube. Free tools: link in bio.

gann-short-A.ig:
Gann's Square of Nine vs random lines.

A hundred-year-old spiral that promises the levels where gold will turn. We tested it: 37,645 level events on micro gold over four sealed years, against 56 sets of fake levels.

About -0.17R per event. 11 versions tested, none passed after correcting for testing that many. Gann ranked below the middle of the fake levels.

Research, not a signal. Not advice.

gann-short-B.ig:
Why Gann levels look like they work.

Draw evenly spaced lines across any market and price will touch some of them. The touches get circled and shared. The lines price sliced through are forgotten.

On last year's micro gold data, price reached at least one Gann level on about 56% of full trading days. Gold's typical day covers about $90, and the levels sit about $60 apart. A touch is not rare.

Illustration on last year's data, not the formal test. Research, not advice.

gann-short-C.ig:
Before you trust a level, do this.

1. Test it against random levels: same days, same trades, same costs.
2. If it cannot clearly beat the random set, it is decoration.
3. Always test on data the rule has never seen.

That last step separates a strategy from a story.

Research, not advice.

Do Nasdaq gaps always fill?

A year of Nasdaq futures, 224 overnight gaps. About 45% filled the same day: 102 of 224. More than half did not.

Size decided it. Gaps under a quarter of a percent filled about 79% of the time. Gaps over 1%, only about 15%.

The saying comes from the small ones.

Past data, not a signal. Research, not advice.

ai-short-C.ig:
Why do AI gold forecasts on social media look so good?

The laziest forecast possible: next close = this close.
On a chart it hugs price beautifully. Its average miss last year: about $7, under 0.2% of the price.
But it never says up or down.

Accuracy and direction are two different scores. Ask what a forecast called, not how close it looks.
